original.title: A tensor has a mathematical meaning and a physical storage description at the same time. Mathematically, it is a scalar, vector, matrix, or higher-dimensional array used in the model computation. Physically, it is a descriptor over storage: shape, dtype, strides, device, layout,
original.disclosure_caption: Tensor properties: shape, dtype, device, layout, and training metadata
original.visible_intro: Shape gives logical dimensions, and dtype gives each element's format. These constrain operation sizes and eligible kernels. Element count times bytes per element gives the logical payload size, while strides, layout, and offset map indices to storage whose allocation can be larger. Device says where storage lives, and training can attach autograd metadata.

original.title: Section 1.2 defined the individual objects. Memory pressure depends on which of those objects overlap in time. Parameters and optimizer buffers may stay live for the whole training step. Saved activations accumulate during forward. Gradients appear during backward. Temporary work
original.disclosure_caption: Live memory in training and serving
original.visible_intro: Parameters are learned weights used in training and inference. Activations are intermediate forward tensors that training may save for backward. Gradients are derivatives of the loss with respect to parameters, and optimizer state holds extra buffers used to update them. Serving can grow a key-value cache of attention keys and values reused during decode. Temporary and communication buffers can raise peak memory.

original.title: Diagnosing a phase requires fixed meanings for the words used to describe speed, because “fast” can refer to one request, a whole service, or one piece of hardware. The rest of the guide uses these meanings:
original.disclosure_caption: Performance measures: latency, throughput, bandwidth, and critical path
original.visible_intro: Latency measures one piece of work, while throughput counts completed work per unit time. A larger batch can improve throughput while raising latency. Bandwidth concerns bytes moved per second. Utilization and saturation need a specified resource, and the critical path sets completion time under fixed dependencies. Measurements here use steady state, after one-time setup, unless stated otherwise.

original.title: GPU memory is not one uniform pool. Performance depends on which level serves the data, who can see it, and how directly the programmer can control it.
original.disclosure_caption: GPU storage levels: registers, shared memory, caches, and HBM
original.visible_intro: Registers belong to individual threads, shared memory is shared within a thread block, L2 cache is shared across the GPU, and HBM holds large device-resident tensors. These levels differ in capacity, speed, and programmer control. High register use per thread can leave room for fewer resident warps on an SM, reducing the GPU's ability to hide waits.

original.title: Allocation state determines whether the next tensor or workspace can be placed without an expensive driver request or an out-of-memory failure. Runtime controls can influence reuse and cache policy, while hardware still decides exact replacement and residency.

Reserved memory is the whole held pool, including cached inactive blocks, so the two figures must not be added. Cache controls express supported intent, while hardware determines actual placement and eviction.

original.title: Calibration chooses quantization parameters from tensors drawn from the expected workload. Hardware support determines whether the GPU and runtime have fast kernels for the chosen format. Offline calibration is needed by static activation quantization and methods such as GPTQ or
original.disclosure_caption: Calibration sets, scales, clipping, and grouping
original.visible_intro: Activation and KV-cache calibration may use representative runtime tensors to choose scales and clipping ranges because their values depend on prompts and model behavior. original.title: Quantization keeps every weight but stores it in fewer bits. Pruning instead removes weights: it sets a chosen subset to zero so that they need not be stored or multiplied. Whether the zeros save time depends on where they fall, because GPU matrix kernels process regular tiles an
original.disclosure_caption: Pruning patterns: unstructured, structured, and 2:4
original.visible_intro: Scattered zero weights need sparse storage and compatible kernels to save work. Removing full rows, columns, or heads can produce smaller dense matrices after related tensors are resized. A 2:4 pattern keeps at most two nonzero weights per four, with hardware gains only on compatible sparse kernels.
